ready2_open_rewrite.resolved_question_text: As shown in the figure, the distance between two smooth parallel metal rails is L, the straight wire MN spans perpendicularly across the rails and is in good contact with the rails, and the entire device is in a uniform magnetic field perpendicular to the plane of the paper inward, with magnetic induction intensity B. The capacitance of the capacitor is C, and except for the resistor R, the resistances of the rails and the wire are all neglected. Now give the wire MN an initial velocity, causing the wire MN to move to the right. After the circuit becomes stable, when MN moves uniformly to the right with speed v, what is the amount of charge carried by the capacitor?
ready2_open_rewrite.resolved_answer: The amount of charge carried by the capacitor is CBLv
ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: Image description: In the figure there are two upper and lower horizontal parallel metal rails; the left-side branch is connected with a capacitor C, and the upper rail on the left side is connected in series with a resistor R; a vertical straight wire MN is perpendicularly connected across the two rails, with M above and N below. The multiple “×” in the figure indicate that the magnetic field is perpendicular to the plane of the paper inward, and the wire MN can move to the right along the rails. Reasoning: The rail spacing is L, the magnetic induction intensity is B, and MN finally moves uniformly to the right with speed v. The wire MN cuts magnetic field lines and produces motional electromotive force, whose magnitude is ε=BLv. After the circuit becomes stable, the capacitor has finished charging, and there is no longer a continuous current in the circuit, so there is no voltage drop across resistor R. Thus the voltage across the capacitor equals the magnitude of the motional electromotive force, namely U=BLv. From the definition of capacitance Q=CU, the magnitude of the charge carried by the capacitor is Q=C·BLv=CBLv.
